_description: Continuity Audit (L10) eval-harness fixture, manuscript 1 of the medium set (LOOM_CONTINUITY_AUDIT.md §21). 'The Long Watch' — a 7-scene science-fiction story aboard a deep-space relay station, with 12 planted contradictions across all four audited classes plus 4 precision-control non-errors. gold_claims score per-scene typed-claim extraction recall; gold_pairs score pairwise adjudication (decoupled from extraction noise); gold_contradictions are the end-to-end findings the whole pipeline should surface, tagged with kind + scene_distance for stratified reporting.
title: The Long Watch

scenes.title: Docking
scenes.prose: The transit pod mated to Relay Station Kessel with a shudder Vint felt in his teeth. Six weeks of empty space behind him, and now this — a grey drum of a station turning slow against the dark. Vint was an inspector for the Bureau of Relays, sent out because Kessel had missed three reporting cycles in a row. He flexed his left hand, the prosthetic one, a Bureau-issue replacement he had never entirely stopped noticing, and waited for the lock to cycle. The station had a single airlock, set on the sunward side where the hull ran warm, and it opened for him grudgingly. Inside, the air was thin and cold and smelled of old electronics. Minimal power: the station had been running dark a long while. Somewhere far off a pump laboured against the quiet. Vint shouldered his kit and stepped through. Whatever had gone wrong aboard Kessel, the silence told him, had been going wrong for months.

scenes.title: The Keeper
scenes.prose: Sael was waiting in the command ring at the station's core, a lean figure with close-cropped silver hair and the stillness that comes of too much solitude. 'You'll be the inspector,' Sael said — not a question. 'Keeper First Class Sael. I've kept Kessel nine years.' The command ring was a curved gallery of dead screens, only a handful still lit; Sael moved among them the way a person crosses their own house in the dark. 'You've had no resupply,' Vint said. 'The last ship came eight months ago,' Sael answered. 'We've made the stores last.' We. Vint marked the word. Sael spoke of the station as though it were crewed still. He asked, mildly, when the trouble had started, and Sael's face closed like a hatch. 'Define trouble,' Sael said, and turned back to the failing screens.

scenes.title: The Reactor
scenes.prose: They went down to the reactor together, two decks below the command ring, through a stairwell where the gravity plating stuttered underfoot. The reactor ran at quarter power, a sullen amber glow behind its shielding. Vint walked the length of the coolant manifold and said little. Sael watched, arms folded, a fresh burn livid across one forearm. 'You handle all the maintenance yourself?' Vint asked. 'There is no one else,' Sael said. On the climb back they passed the medical bay, and its hatch was sealed — a red lockplate, a door that would not give. Sael offered nothing, and Vint did not yet press. A station gave up its secrets in its own order; he had learned that much.

scenes.title: Orsa's Bunk
scenes.prose: In the crew quarters most bunks were stripped to the bare frame, but one still held a blanket and a row of taped-up star charts. It had been Orsa's — the station technician, who had left Kessel a year ago on the last tender. 'She kept those charts like scripture,' Sael said from the hatchway. Vint touched the edge of one. Kessel had carried a crew of twelve once; he had read that much in the Bureau file. 'Whoever cut that coolant line,' Vint said quietly, 'knew this station's schematics by heart.' Sael let that pass. 'I called the Bureau in myself,' the keeper added, 'the moment things began to turn' — and that was the first thing Vint did not believe, for he had been sent because Kessel went silent, not because it called. The blanket on Orsa's bunk was folded with a care no empty room earns.

scenes.title: The Log
scenes.prose: Sael's quarters were small and scrupulously kept. The keeper called up the station log on a cracked handscreen and, for the first time, did not look away from him. 'Kessler Relay has not had a clean year since I took it,' Sael said — and Vint, an inspector for the Bureau of Relays, kept his face still and let the keeper talk. 'Six years I've kept this station. The supply tender last came three months back. And the coolant line —' Sael stopped. 'I cut it. Then I logged a fault, and I never told the Bureau. Nine weeks it took you to reach me, and I spent every one of them deciding whether to say so.' The handscreen's light shook a little. 'There. Now you have it.'

scenes.title: Shadow Side
scenes.prose: Vint needed air that did not taste of Sael's confession, and the station gave him a second airlock on the shadow side, cold enough that his breath ghosted at the viewport. He turned a stylus over in his right hand — the prosthetic, its metal dulled by years of handling. Sael found him there. 'You'll report all of it,' the keeper said. A junior keeper learned early that the Bureau forgave nothing, and Sael had never risen past that rank. 'Orsa is well out of it,' Sael added quietly. It had been half a year since Orsa left. Below the viewport the dark turned, slow and entire.

scenes.title: The Watch
scenes.prose: They kept the last watch together in the command ring, which on Kessel was the outermost deck, a band of dark glass against the turning stars. The reactor sat above them now, up on the ring's spine, and through the deckhead Vint could hear it idling low, barely lit. Sael had pushed back the hood of the work-suit, and the deck light caught the keeper's dark hair and the old burn on one forearm, scabbed over now and fading. 'You could have run,' Vint said. 'Nine years is a long time to then run,' Sael answered. Vint logged the station as failing but salvageable, and the keeper as the same. When the relief ship came he would be aboard it; until then there was the watch, and the reactor's small light, and the cold.
